A [standard deviation](../random-variables-and-distributions/standard-deviation.qmd) can be defined for any random variable having finite variance. A **standard error** applies that same definition to an estimator. So the phrase tells us which random variable has the spread: we are measuring how the estimator varies across repeated samples. We continue with the nonparametric bootstrap of the Hillenbrand cohort introduced on the [estimator page](properties-of-estimators.qmd#estimators-are-random-variables).

We will derive the standard error of a sample mean under independence and compare the formula with empirical speaker resamples. Once the agreement is visible, we can ask which dependence and target assumptions make that formula appropriate for a particular analysis.

## Deriving the standard error of a mean

If $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ are independent with common variance $\sigma^2$, then

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Var}[\overline X]
&=\operatorname{Var}[\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^nX_i]\\
&=\frac{1}{n^2}\left(
\sum_{i=1}^n\operatorname{Var}[X_i]
+2\sum_{i<j}\operatorname{Cov}[X_i,X_j]
\right)\\
&=\frac{1}{n^2}\sum_{i=1}^n\operatorname{Var}[X_i]\\
&=\frac{\sigma^2}{n}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus

$$
\operatorname{SE}(\overline X)=\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}.
$$

The third equality uses [independence](../foundations/independence.qmd): independence implies zero covariance, so the pairwise covariance sum vanishes. With dependent observations, those terms remain. Positive within-speaker or within-document covariance typically makes the independent-row formula too small. This is the variance decomposition introduced on the [variance-and-covariance page](../random-variables-and-distributions/variance-and-covariance.qmd#covariance-and-a-variance-decomposition).

## Checking the relation in vowel durations

The four sample sizes below are not arbitrary: they are the observed counts of girls, boys, men, and women in Hillenbrand et al.'s speaker cohort. The duration distribution remains the adult-women /I/ distribution so that only $n$ changes.

```{r}
#| label: hillenbrand-standard-errors
library(ggplot2)

vowels <- read.csv(
  "data/hillenbrand/vowels-complete.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
women_hid <- subset(vowels, speaker_type == "woman" & vowel == "I")
x <- women_hid$duration_ms
sigma <- sqrt(mean((x - mean(x))^2))

speaker_rows <- unique(vowels[c("speaker_id", "speaker_type")])
sample_sizes <- sort(as.integer(table(speaker_rows$speaker_type)))

set.seed(20261018)
replicates <- 20000L
se_table <- do.call(rbind, lapply(sample_sizes, function(n) {
  estimates <- replicate(replicates, mean(sample(x, n, replace = TRUE)))
  data.frame(
    sample_size = n,
    simulated_se_ms = sd(estimates),
    analytic_se_ms = sigma / sqrt(n)
  )
}))

stopifnot(max(abs(se_table$simulated_se_ms - se_table$analytic_se_ms)) < 0.15)
se_table
```

```{r}
#| label: plot-hillenbrand-standard-errors
#| fig-cap: "Bootstrap standard errors (points) and analytic values under the empirical distribution (line)."
ggplot(se_table, aes(sample_size, analytic_se_ms)) +
  geom_line(color = "#8B1A1A", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(aes(y = simulated_se_ms), color = "grey25", size = 2.2) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = sample_sizes) +
  labs(x = "Resampled speakers", y = "Standard error of mean duration (ms)") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

At the observed adult-women sample size, the simulation gives `r sprintf("%.3f", se_table$simulated_se_ms[se_table$sample_size == nrow(women_hid)])` ms, compared with the analytic value `r sprintf("%.3f", se_table$analytic_se_ms[se_table$sample_size == nrow(women_hid)])` ms.

When $\sigma$ is unknown, ordinary data analysis substitutes the sample standard deviation $s$:

$$
\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}(\overline X)=\frac{s}{\sqrt n}.
$$

The square-root relation means that precision improves more slowly than the row count. But adding dependent rows need not follow this relation at all.

## Recap and forward link

1. The response standard deviation describes variation among $X_i$ values; the standard error describes variation in $T(\mathbf X)$ across samples.
2. The formula $\sigma/\sqrt n$ follows only after the covariance terms are set to zero.
3. In practice, $s/\sqrt n$ estimates the unknown standard error; $s$ and $\sigma$ are not the same object.

The [bias page](estimator-bias.qmd) next turns from the spread of a sampling distribution to its center.

## Check your understanding

1. Which line in the derivation requires independence?
2. Why are the plotted sample sizes data-derived?
3. How would positive within-speaker covariance affect a naive row-level standard error?
4. Distinguish the response standard deviation from the standard error of the mean.

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. The step from the variance of a sum to the sum of variances omits covariance terms and thus requires independence. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. The plotted sample sizes are the observed Hillenbrand cohort sizes: 19 girls, 27 boys, 45 men, and 48 women. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. Positive covariance would add positive terms to the variance of the mean, so a row-independent standard error would tend to be too small. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. The response standard deviation describes variation among individual durations; the standard error describes variation of the sample mean across samples. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->

</details>
